articleTitle: DSP literacy: a must for first-year engineering students
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: At the Polytechnic of Central London (PCL), there is a very strong emphasis on DSP with all-through study provision starting at first-year undergraduate level on to an MSc in digital signal processing systems and PhD-level research. The authors focus on just one part of this scenario: the BEng undergraduate programme, in which DSP accounts for around 15% of the total study programme. This consistent emphasis on DSP provides an excellent vehicle for promoting a systems-level viewpoint, underpinned by a fairly demanding design/analysis approach, which relates comfortably to the study of allied topics such as microelectronics, where nowadays a hierarchical top-down conceptualization/bottom-up understanding procedural framework is essential. The authors describe the modules taught in each year of the course and then discuss the first year of the course in more detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Approaches to DSP in the School of Engineering Information Technology at Sheffield City Polytechnic, 1984-90
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The authors discuss the evolution of the methods used to teach DSP as part of a more general course on signal processing. More particularly, they focus on the topics of correlation, spectral analysis, and digital filter design. This subject is introduced in the final year only of the Honours/Degree Course on Electronic Systems and Control Engineering. The authors discuss the aims, history, observed problems, and the attempted solutions to these problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The key points that could be addressed by lecturers engaged in DSP teaching practice at universities and polytechnics are presented. The following important considerations are discussed: students' prerequisite knowledge; course content; depth of treatment; teaching and tutorial materials; methods of presentation; knowledge consolidation and feedback; intellectual challenge; practical investigations; case studies; projects; assessment of knowledge and understanding; and curriculum development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Conceptual tools for signal processing systems analysis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: Signal processing is the extraction of relevant data by the exploitation of external information or postulates regarding: the input signal, its noise and interference environment, and the nature and intended use of the output data. Successful implementations do not depend primarily on advanced mathematical techniques and powerful processors. Only a clear visualization of the input scenario and of the output application can reveal those features of the signal and interference, and that a priori information can be exploited to enhance the output function. The key challenge is the strategic decision of what to do, not the tactic of how to do it. The author gives a simple introduction to some of the pertinent strategic principles. The author discusses signal space and state space, feature matching, weighted coherent signal summation, application dependent weighting, and limiting conditions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The authors describe the experience of Bradford University in the teaching of applied signal processing. The environment in which the DSP module is to be designed is described and the appropriateness of theoretical and practical approaches are discussed. The course implementation at Bradford, including the organisation of practical exercises, is described. In addition to an assessment of DSP laboratory hardware, the issue of 'what DSP language?' is addressed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An industry perspective of recruiting graduate engineers for DSP research
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: It is not an easy task to recruit graduate engineers for DSP research. In order to be effective in such research, an engineer must possess a range of capabilities which encompasses factual knowledge concerning the availability of state-of-the-art devices and a mathematical ability that is firmly based on a physical understanding of processing problems. Newly graduated engineers are typically well versed in the design and construction of DSP modules to perform specified algorithms using an appropriate combination of dedicated and programmable logic devices. It is in the area of the application of mathematical techniques and physical reasoning to the analysis and development of algorithms that most on-the-job training is required. The authors discuss the relevance of these skills in DSP research and the related requirement for engineers to be able to communicate effectively the results of their research to colleagues and customers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 'Teach yourself' signal processing at University College London
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The author describes a set of 'teach yourself' tutorial guides used by undergraduates in the Department of Electronic and Electrical Engineering at University College London. The tutorials are based on the PC MATLAB matrix and vector handling package and students work through them in their own time. Their use in the teaching of sampled signals in digital signal processing is discussed. They provide a working knowledge of sampled signals and spectra and of data filtering and smoothing, including a statistical goodness-of-fit test for model validation. The advanced material reinforces lecture courses by providing graphical visualisations of convolution, sampled data systems and the z-transform. The author presents examples of teaching material and exercises from the tutorials, but first discusses their context within an overall strategy for student education and development in electronic and electrical engineering, which is ultimately shaped by the IEE accreditation requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of signal processing workstations to the teaching of undergraduates and postgraduates
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: In the maritime environment there is considerable use of sonar, radar, communications, power and control systems. All of these systems employ digital signal processing activities in the achievement of their tasks. It is therefore prudent for the Royal Naval engineering College (RNEC) to continue to ensure that its graduate engineers are fully prepared with an appreciation of all aspects of signal processing. To this end a PC based signal processing workstation has been implemented. The authors describe the system and its typical functions. The authors discuss two applications of the workstation, these are the building of a DSP automatic voltage regulator and speed governor control loop, and an adaptive filter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A simple approach to the teaching of DSP
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The teaching of DSP tended to become algorithmically very mathematical as the subject evolved into an autonomous discipline but the relevance of this approach is questionable when the undergraduates concerned are largely interested in control engineering or seismology. Those studying a multidisciplinary engineering course may well have a basic grounding in electronics and also in real time and embedded computing. This is the case for Southampton Institute's BSc in Industrial Systems Technology. Open University undergraduates are often following multidisciplinary profiles and in this respect the challenge to staff at both institutions had an element of commonality. The objectives of the two course teams were different and this is reflected in the approaches taken. The authors describe these two approaches.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Teaching DSP to engineers on post-experience courses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: The Sonar and Underwater Group of the School of Electronic and Electrical Engineering at Birmingham University have run a post-experience course in Sonar and Underwater Acoustics. The course lasts for two weeks. Underwater acoustics and general sonar principles are covered in the first week, while signal processing is the subject of the second week. The authors describe the way in which the signal processing material is taught and the experiences gained in running the course. The relevance of this activity to the teaching of DSP to undergraduates in the university is discussed so that lessons can be learnt that will benefit both activities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital signal processing requirements for engineers in defence research: research areas for next generation systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: Digital signal processing (DSP) systems used in existing military applications are significantly more powerful than those used in most commercial applications: typical military DSP systems are capable of calculating several hundred million arithmetic operations per second. At least three orders of magnitude increase in computing power are required to maintain a viable system capability in the 1990s, when typical applications will need throughputs approaching one million, million arithmetic operations per second. Increases of this order require simultaneous advances in several of the technology areas that underpin DSP. The author discusses some of the DSP-related problems in these areas and outlines the research effort and engineering skills required to maintain a useful system capability. The author gives a brief history of the development of semiconductor technology and its application to DSP. Future developments to increase the number of arithmetic operations per second are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Matching academic requirements and component suppliers resources
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of DSP in Universities and Polytechnics
abstract: There is a challenge for educators to provide the skills and the insight to students to allow them to contribute fully to the growing DSP revolution. The theoretical basis of DSP is often well covered in degree courses, what is usually lacking is instruction in how to apply this knowledge. Texas Instruments (TI), and other DSP vendors, wish to help to provide facilities for the practical teaching of DSP. This is partly through an altruistic desire to educate the UK engineering community in the benefits of DSP, though clearly there are other benefits which make the financial investment worthwhile. The wish to see a greater practical content is DSP teaching has caused TI to introduce a wide range of educational support. The author discusses the support provided by TI and the benefits to the student and vendor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
